title: Split semisimple root decomposition and simple root generators
statement:
Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $\mathbf Q$ [def-wf-lie-algebra], semisimple in the sense of having no nonzero solvable ideal [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra]. Let $\mathfrak h$ be a maximal abelian subalgebra such that all $\operatorname{ad}(h)$ are diagonalizable over $\mathbf Q$. Put $\mathfrak g_\alpha=\{x:[h,x]=\alpha(h)x	ext{ for all }h\in\mathfrak h\}$ for $\alpha\in\mathfrak h^\vee$ and $R=\{\alpha
e0:\mathfrak g_\alpha
e0\}$. Then $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus igoplus_{\alpha\in R}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, every $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ for $\alpha\in R$ is one-dimensional, and $[\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}]$ is a line in $\mathfrak h$ containing a unique $h_\alpha$ with $\alpha(h_\alpha)=2$. The families $(\alpha,h_\alpha)$ form a finite reduced crystallographic root pairing for the evaluation pairing $\mathfrak h^\vee	imes\mathfrak h	o\mathbf Q$: both families span, every $ eta(h_\alpha)$ is an integer, $R\cap\mathbf Q\alpha=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$, and the maps $s_\alpha(\xi)=\xi-\xi(h_\alpha)\alpha$ and $s_\alpha^\vee(h)=h-\alpha(h)h_\alpha$ permute the two families with the same permutation. The group generated by the $s_\alpha$ is finite. If $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\}\subseteq R$ is a rational basis of $\mathfrak h^\vee$ in which every root has sign-coherent integer coordinates, put $R^+=R\cap\mathbf Z_{\ge0}\Delta$ and $\mathfrak n^\pm= igoplus_{\alpha\in R^+}\mathfrak g_{\pm\alpha}$. For any nonzero $e_i\in\mathfrak g_{\alpha_i}$ there is $f_i\in\mathfrak g_{-\alpha_i}$ with $[e_i,f_i]=h_{\alpha_i}$, $[h_{\alpha_i},e_i]=2e_i$, $[h_{\alpha_i},f_i]=-2f_i$, and $[e_i,f_j]=0$ for $i
e j$. The subalgebras $\mathfrak n^+$ and $\mathfrak n^-$ are generated as Lie algebras by the $e_i$ and the $f_i$, respectively. For every nonzero root vector $x\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$, $\operatorname{ad}(x)$ is nilpotent on $\mathfrak g$. When $\mathfrak g=0$ the root sets and generating families are empty.

proof.text: The radical is zero by [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra], so [sk-lem-walg-killing] makes $B$ nondegenerate. The abelian $\mathfrak h$ is nilpotent. If $x$ normalizes $\mathfrak h$, then $(\operatorname{ad}h)^2x=0$ for every $h\in\mathfrak h$, since $[h,x]\in\mathfrak h$. In a diagonal basis, $T^2x=0$ implies $Tx=0$, so $x$ centralizes $\mathfrak h$. Then $\mathfrak h+\mathbf Qx$ is abelian, hence equals $\mathfrak h$ by maximality. Thus $\mathfrak h$ is self-normalizing, and is a Cartan subalgebra in the nilpotent self-normalizing sense. Its diagonal adjoint actions are triangularizable over $\mathbf Q$.

source.place: Section 23h, printed p.503 (splitting Cartan and root decomposition), pp.508--509 (rank-one triples); Appendix C, pp.609--612 (simple bases). Expanded argument by Q75.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-nilpotent-module-generalized-weight-decomposition] to the adjoint representation of $\mathfrak h$ on $\mathfrak g$. Each adjoint operator is diagonalizable, so its generalized $a$-eigenspace is its ordinary $a$-eigenspace: in a diagonal basis $(T-a)^nx=0$ forces every coordinate with eigenvalue different from $a$ to vanish. Thus every simultaneous generalized space is an ordinary one. A nonzero vector in such a space forces its weight to be linear by $[ah+bk,x]=a[h,x]+b[k,x]$. The zero space is the centralizer of $\mathfrak h$, which equals $\mathfrak h$ by the maximal-abelian argument of step 1. Independence, spanning, and finite support in the cited node give the claimed finite root decomposition, including $\mathfrak g=0$.

source.place: Section 23h, printed p.503 (splitting Cartan and root decomposition), pp.508--509 (rank-one triples); Appendix C, pp.609--612 (simple bases). Expanded argument by Q75.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-killing-cartan-rank-one-spaces] to the Cartan subalgebra of step 1. Its hypotheses hold over $\mathbf Q$; step 2 identifies its generalized root spaces with the $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ here. Every nonzero root space has dimension one. The cited triple $u_\alpha,v_\alpha,c_\alpha$ gives a nonzero bracket in $\mathfrak h$ with $\alpha(c_\alpha)=2$. Since both root spaces are lines, all their brackets are multiples of this bracket. Hence $[\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}]=\mathbf Qc_\alpha$ and there is exactly one element of this line on which $\alpha$ is $2$. This identifies $h_\alpha=c_\alpha$. Now [lem-sfb-killing-cartan-reduced-root-pairing], with the same Killing-dual formula for $c_\alpha$, gives both spanning families, all integral pairings, reducedness and the simultaneous reflection permutations.

source.place: Section 23h, printed p.503 (splitting Cartan and root decomposition), pp.508--509 (rank-one triples); Appendix C, pp.609--612 (simple bases). Expanded argument by Q75.

proof.text: The reflection group acts on the finite set $R$. If an element of the group fixes every root, it fixes their rational span, which is all of $\mathfrak h^\vee$ by step 3; thus it is the identity. This embeds the group into the finite permutation group of $R$, proving finiteness, also when $R=\varnothing$.

source.place: Section 23h, printed p.503 (splitting Cartan and root decomposition), pp.508--509 (rank-one triples); Appendix C, pp.609--612 (simple bases). Expanded argument by Q75.

proof.text: For a prescribed $e_i\ne0$, write $e_i=a_i u_{\alpha_i}$ with $a_i\in\mathbf Q^\times$ using step 3, and put $f_i=a_i^{-1}v_{\alpha_i}$. Bilinearity gives $[e_i,f_i]=h_{\alpha_i}$ and the two remaining rank-one identities. Jacobi gives $[\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_\beta]\subseteq\mathfrak g_{\alpha+\beta}$ by $[h,[x,y]]=(\alpha(h)+\beta(h))[x,y]$. If $i\ne j$, the difference $\alpha_i-\alpha_j$ is nonzero and has mixed-sign basis coordinates, so is not a root. Therefore $[e_i,f_j]=0$. The same weight identity shows that the sums defining $\mathfrak n^\pm$ are Lie subalgebras: sums of two strictly positive, respectively negative, weights cannot be zero and have the required sign whenever they are roots.

source.place: Section 23h, printed p.503 (splitting Cartan and root decomposition), pp.508--509 (rank-one triples); Appendix C, pp.609--612 (simple bases). Expanded argument by Q75.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-root-base-rational-integral-spans] with the reduced crystallographic evaluation pairing from step 3 and $J=\Delta\subseteq R$. Rational linear independence and sign-coherent integral root expansions are precisely its hypotheses. It gives independence of the simple coroots and sign-coherent integral coroot expansions. Consequently these roots and coroots, with support $\Delta$, form a base in the sense explicitly defined in [lem-sfb-positive-root-word-partial-sums]. For each $\gamma\in R^+$ that node supplies a sequence of simple roots with sum $\gamma$ and every nonempty partial sum a root. Each partial sum is positive, since its simple-root coordinates are nonnegative.

source.place: Section 23h, printed p.503 (splitting Cartan and root decomposition), pp.508--509 (rank-one triples); Appendix C, pp.609--612 (simple bases). Expanded argument by Q75.

proof.text: Let $E$ be the Lie subalgebra generated by the $e_i$. It lies in $\mathfrak n^+$ by step 5. For a root word $\delta_0,\ldots,\delta_{n-1}$ supplied by step 6, $n>0$ since its sum is the nonzero root $\gamma$. Start with $z_0=e_{\delta_0}$ and recursively put $z_k=[z_{k-1},e_{\delta_k}]$. By induction, $z_{k-1}$ has the nonzero partial-sum weight, and [lem-sfb-nonopposite-root-bracket-nonvanishing] says $z_k\ne0$, since the next partial sum is again a nonzero root. All its hypotheses (characteristic zero, finite dimension, Killing form, diagonal splitting Cartan) were established in steps 1--3. At the last stage $z_{n-1}\in E\cap\mathfrak g_\gamma$ is nonzero, hence spans this one-dimensional space. Thus $E$ contains every positive root space, proving $E=\mathfrak n^+$. Using $f_{\delta_k}$ and the negatives of the same partial sums proves generation of $\mathfrak n^-$. Empty root systems give zero generated subalgebras.

source.place: Section 23h, printed p.503 (splitting Cartan and root decomposition), pp.508--509 (rank-one triples); Appendix C, pp.609--612 (simple bases). Expanded argument by Q75.

proof.text: Fix $\alpha\in R$ and $x\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$. Put $S=R\cup\{0\}$. Repeated use of the Jacobi weight identity in step 5 gives $(\operatorname{ad}x)^N\mathfrak g_\beta\subseteq\mathfrak g_{\beta+N\alpha}$, also for $\beta=0$ and $\mathfrak g_0=\mathfrak h$. For each pair $\beta,\eta\in S$, the equation $\beta+N\alpha=\eta$ has at most one integer solution because $\alpha\ne0$. Choose a positive integer $N$ outside this finite collection. Every target space then vanishes by definition of $R$, so the decomposition of step 2 implies $(\operatorname{ad}x)^N=0$ on $\mathfrak g$. This proves nilpotence for all nonzero root vectors as required.
